interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Self-Calibrating Dense Displacement Fields for Reliable Co-Registration of Large Optical Satellite Imagery
papers.authors: Shoukun Sun , Zhe Wang , Sanaz Salati , Jiyin Zhang , Hui Wang , Xiaogang Ma
papers.abstract: Co-registration underlies nearly every multi-temporal and multi-sensor use of optical satellite imagery, and operational products still carry documented offsets well above the fraction-of-a-pixel scale at which change detection, time series, and data fusion degrade. Real image pairs differ along several axes at once (sensor response, scene content, viewing geometry, resolution, mosaic seams), and the last of these is not a single global motion. Existing tools embed a motion model and constants tuned to their development data; a pair that fits is registered precisely, while one that does not either fails to match or returns a result wrong by tens of pixels with no failure reported. Learned matchers add a GPU requirement and carry no accuracy guarantee outside their training distribution. We present SCDF (self-calibrating displacement fields), a training-free, GPU-free estimator whose motion model is the dense per-pixel displacement field itself, so no scene motion falls outside the model. A single predict--measure--filter loop runs over a resolution pyramid: the accumulated field predicts where each patch of the moving image falls in the reference, RootSIFT matching and a correlation pass measure the displacement there to sub-pixel precision, and filters whose thresholds are all calibrated on the image pair itself decide what survives. One configuration, with no per-dataset tuning, processes full $8192^2$ scenes on a single CPU core. On 584 constructed-ground-truth pairs built from real Sentinel-2, Landsat-8/9, and NAIP imagery, against seven classical baselines and two zero-shot pretrained matchers, SCDF registers every pair with zero failures, reduces the best baseline's real-pair median end-point error from 6.83 to 4.17m, and cuts its 90th percentile from 17.8 to 7.77m.
papers.Reasons for match: The paper's self-calibrating dense displacement fields for satellite image co-registration is highly relevant to astronomical image alignment, especially for multi-wavelength or multi-epoch data.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses co-registration of large optical satellite imagery, proposing a training-free, GPU-free method that estimates dense per-pixel displacement fields without a fixed motion model. The main idea is to use a predict-measure-filter loop over a resolution pyramid with self-calibrated thresholds. This matters for astronomy because it could be applied to align JWST, HST, or survey images, improving change detection and data fusion. The method is robust and requires no tuning, making it attractive for large datasets.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is tested on images with different sensors or resolutions, similar to astronomical multi-instrument data.
Look for details on sub-pixel accuracy and failure modes that might affect astronomical images.

papers.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
papers.authors: Seth Karten , Alex L. Zhang , Kevin Thomas , Sebastian Müller , Elie Bakouch , Daniel Auras , Mika Senghaas , Fares Obeid , Konstantin Dunas , Johannes Hagemann , Sami Jaghouar
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
papers.abstract: Language models are sequential processors, but long-horizon agency requires external information and computation beyond model weights and active context. Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. A persistent IPython REPL follows the Recursive Language Model abstraction for programmatic context processing and test-time compute, while Continual Harness preserves histories, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications across trajectories. Recursive subagents coordinate through direct agent-to-agent communication, and the Agents View lets humans inspect and manage daemon-backed sessions. Prime Agent standardizes execution, recovery, verification, and resource accounting while leaving strategy construction to the model. This low-friction, expressive membrane prevents harness failures from becoming model failures and pushes measurement toward the model's true maximal underlying capability. Prime Agent raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5% and matches or exceeds native and popular harnesses across long-context coding, GPU-kernel generation, emulator construction, and autonomous nanoGPT speedruns. On Factorio, we find refinement allows for continuous technology progression and dedicated subagents enable parallelized work. Code is available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to LLM agents for coding and long-horizon scientific workflows, with a self-improving harness that could be adapted for automated data analysis in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces Prime Agent, an open-source harness for long-horizon coding-agent workflows that uses a persistent IPython REPL and recursive subagents to manage context and computation. It improves performance on ARC-AGI-3 and other tasks by standardizing execution and recovery, while leaving strategy to the model. For astronomy, this could enable autonomous pipelines for JWST data reduction or spectral fitting, where long-running tasks and error recovery are common. I could imagine using it to run reproducible end-to-end analyses on large survey catalogs. However, its focus on coding benchmarks means I should check whether its abstractions handle domain-specific tools like astropy or CASA efficiently.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the harness supports custom tool integration (e.g., astropy, JWST pipeline) and how it handles external data I/O.
Look for details on subagent communication and whether it can parallelize independent spectral fits or image analyses.
Assess the resource accounting and recovery mechanisms for long-running astronomical computations.

papers.title: Beyond Sparse Weights: When Is Attention Compressible?
papers.abstract: KV-cache compression is often justified by attention maps with a few large weights. This is incomplete: large weights may not contain most of the mass, omitted values can cancel, and preserving the attention output may not preserve the task. We separate these questions. Global score gaps -- not threshold counts -- determine how many tokens are needed to retain a target mass. For a realized row, the weighted sum of omitted values is the exact missing statistic. A controlled retrieval--aggregation model explains when truncation helps and when it hurts. These results motivate CertKV, a training-free compressor that reserves one tail-summary slot per head and allocates the rest by value dispersion. Under matched budgets, CertKV is top-two in seven of nine LongBench-v2 settings, remains in the leading compressed tier on 128K RULER, and realizes a ten-fold cache budget in a packed Llama prototype. Compressibility depends on the mass, values, future queries, and task -- not on a sparse-looking map alone.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses KV-cache compression in LLMs, which is relevant to efficient inference for large models used in astronomical data analysis. The training-free compressor and analysis of attention compressibility could transfer to managing long context in research agents or processing large catalogs.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks when attention maps in LLMs are truly compressible for KV-cache reduction, challenging the common assumption that sparse-looking attention implies easy compression. It introduces CertKV, a training-free compressor that reserves a tail-summary slot per head and allocates remaining budget by value dispersion, achieving strong performance on LongBench and RULER benchmarks. For astronomy, this could enable running large language models on limited hardware for tasks like literature review or code generation with long contexts. A concrete workflow could be compressing KV-cache in an LLM-based agent that processes long JWST observation logs or multi-wavelength catalogs. Before investing, check whether the method's assumptions hold for attention patterns in domain-specific prompts and whether the performance gains persist on astronomical text.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if CertKV's tail-summary slot mechanism is described with pseudocode or algorithm details
Look for ablation studies on different attention patterns or sequence lengths
Verify if the method is tested on tasks beyond LongBench and RULER, such as code or scientific text
Inspect whether the paper discusses memory savings and latency improvements in practical deployments

papers.title: GeoQ: Geometry-Aware Conditional Quantile Error Estimation for Scientific Surrogate Models
papers.authors: Khoa Nguyen , Daniel Serino , Aviral Prakash , Marc Klasky
papers.abstract: Neural-network surrogate models are increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulations, but their deployment in extrapolative and autoregressive settings requires input-dependent estimates of prediction error. In this work, we introduce GeoQ (Geometry-Aware Conditional Quantile Error Estimation), a non-intrusive calibration framework for estimating surrogate error at individual query points. GeoQ represents the error at a query point as an anchor-averaged calibration error plus a learned nonnegative correction. This correction is modeled as an upper conditional quantile of the anchor-relative error increment, using geometry-based features that encode representation-space displacement and local support density. A cross-fitting procedure generates approximately out-of-sample calibration tuples, while a feature-space k-nearest-neighbor support score identifies regions \textcolor{black}{where the learned error model is supported by calibration data}. We evaluate GeoQ on scalar regression, chaotic dynamics, medium-range weather forecasting, and Richtmyer-Meshkov instability prediction. The results demonstrate that geometry-aware conditional quantile modeling provides a practical and non-intrusive approach for validity-aware error estimation in scientific surrogate models.
papers.Reasons for match: Focuses on uncertainty estimation for neural surrogate models, which is directly relevant to astronomical source classification and SED fitting where reliable error bars are crucial. The non-intrusive calibration approach could transfer to JWST data analysis workflows.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the need for input-dependent error estimates in neural-network surrogate models used for scientific simulations. It introduces GeoQ, a calibration framework that estimates prediction error at individual query points using geometry-based features and conditional quantile modeling. This matters for astronomy because JWST and survey data analysis often relies on surrogate models where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. The method could be applied to photometric redshift estimation or SED fitting to provide more reliable error bars. However, the paper's evaluation is on physical simulations, so transfer to astronomical data would require testing on domain-specific surrogates.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is demonstrated on regression tasks similar to photometric redshift or SED fitting
Look for details on how the k-nearest-neighbor support score handles sparse data regions
See if the cross-fitting procedure is computationally feasible for large astronomical datasets

papers.title: DAW: Dynamics-Aware Weighting for Deep Learning Forecasts of Chaotic Systems
papers.abstract: Deep learning surrogates for forecasting chaotic dynamical systems suffer from catastrophic error accumulation over long-term autoregressive rollouts. This behavior is partly tied to the underlying systems: chaotic spatiotemporal systems, such as the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, visit phase space unevenly - dominated by recurrent, low-dimensional quiescent states (e.g., near-laminar flows) and punctuated by rare, dynamically complex topological transitions (e.g., wave-merging events). Under a sample-wise uniform objective, standard neural surrogates allocate their finite capacity to the statistically numerous quiescent states, under-representing the transient regimes that trigger disproportionate, localized errors. Existing imbalanced-regression methods reweight samples by target-space density. However, statistical target-space rarity need not coincide with the intrinsic dynamical rarity - the recurrence geometry of the attractor that is the source of the imbalance. To address this, we introduce Dynamics-Aware Weighting (DAW), a data-centric objective reweighting framework. Using the local dimension $d$ from dynamical systems theory as an a priori measure of a state's active degrees of freedom, DAW reshapes the loss landscape to allocate representational capacity toward the sparse, high-$d$ regimes where forecast errors are systematically large. On the chaotic KS equation, DAW consistently outperforms uniform training, purely statistical density weighting, and its randomly permuted ablation, reducing long-term autoregressive error relative to all baselines. Event-level analysis shows that DAW achieves this by suppressing the localized error amplifications incurred during sharp jumps in $d$, which accompany complex physical processes such as wave-merging in the KS system.
papers.Reasons for match: The method of dynamics-aware weighting for chaotic systems could transfer to astronomical time-series or dynamical modeling, though the direct application is not astronomy-specific.
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses error accumulation in deep learning forecasts of chaotic systems, proposing a weighting scheme based on local dimension from dynamical systems theory. The main idea is to reweight training samples to focus on rare, high-dimensional states that cause large errors. This could matter for astronomy in forecasting or modeling chaotic astrophysical processes, but requires adaptation to specific problems like stellar variability or gravitational wave signals.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is tested on systems beyond Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, such as astronomical dynamical systems.
Look for details on how local dimension is computed and whether it is feasible for large astronomical datasets.
